title: Jeremiah 16:1–13
context: Jeremiah reports the LORD's word to him. The LORD forbids him to marry or have children in Judah, to enter a house of mourning, or to join a house of feasting. These sign-acts embody the coming disaster: so many will die that there will be no proper burial or mourning, and all joy, including the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, will cease. When the people ask why, Jeremiah is to answer that their fathers forsook the LORD and that they have done even worse, following their own stubborn hearts. The LORD will cast them out of the land.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: "Then the LORD’s word came to me, saying." Arminian readers note that Jeremiah is the speaker reporting the LORD's word. His own life is about to become a message to the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the word comes from the LORD himself, not from Jeremiah's own judgment. The prophet's personal choices are placed under God's command for the sake of his people.

verses.text: “You shall not take a wife, neither shall you have sons or daughters, in this place.”
verses.arminianNotes: "You shall not take a wife, neither shall you have sons or daughters, in this place." Arminian readers see a costly obedience: Jeremiah gives up marriage and family as a living warning of the coming judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this command was unusual in Israel, where marriage and children were seen as blessings. Jeremiah's single life becomes a sign. Paul's counsel in 1 Corinthians 7:26 is sometimes compared, though its setting differs.

verses.text: For the LORD says concerning the sons and concerning the daughters who are born in this place, and concerning their mothers who bore them, and concerning their fathers who became their father in this land:
verses.arminianNotes: "For the LORD says concerning the sons and concerning the daughters who are born in this place." Arminian readers see that the command is explained by what will happen to families in the land, not by any fault in marriage itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD names sons, daughters, mothers, and fathers. Every part of family life in Judah will be touched by the judgment, which is why Jeremiah must not start a family there.

verses.text: “They will die grievous deaths. They will not be lamented, neither will they be buried. They will be as dung on the surface of the ground. They will be consumed by the sword and by famine. Their dead bodies will be food for the birds of the sky and for the animals of the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: "They will die grievous deaths." Arminian readers see the horror of judgment: no lament, no burial, bodies left "as dung on the surface of the ground," consumed by sword and famine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal of the dignity normally given the dead. Being left unburied for the birds and animals was a mark of curse. The LORD's warning is severe because the sin is grave.

verses.text: For the LORD says, “Don’t enter into the house of mourning. Don’t go to lament. Don’t bemoan them, for I have taken away my peace from this people,” says the LORD, “even loving kindness and tender mercies.
verses.arminianNotes: "Don’t enter into the house of mourning." Arminian readers see Jeremiah forbidden to comfort mourners because the LORD has "taken away my peace from this people," a sign that judgment has come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD withdraws "loving kindness and tender mercies." The covenant blessings Israel enjoyed are being taken away. Both traditions read this as a solemn judicial act, not arbitrary harshness.

verses.text: Both great and small will die in this land. They will not be buried. Men won’t lament for them, cut themselves, or make themselves bald for them.
verses.arminianNotes: "Both great and small will die in this land." Arminian readers see that no social rank will protect anyone, and the customary rites of grief will be left undone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that cutting oneself and shaving the head for the dead were forbidden in Israel's law (Deuteronomy 14:1). The verse describes practices people would have done, without endorsing them.

verses.text: Men won’t break bread for them in mourning, to comfort them for the dead. Men won’t give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father or for their mother.
verses.arminianNotes: "Men won’t break bread for them in mourning." Arminian readers see even the simple comforts of grief, the shared meal and "the cup of consolation," disappearing under the weight of the disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the loss of these rites shows how complete the judgment will be. Grief itself will have no comfort. Both traditions read the verse as part of the sign-act's meaning.

verses.text: “You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them, to eat and to drink.”
verses.arminianNotes: "You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them." Arminian readers see the second half of the sign: Jeremiah refuses both mourning and celebration, because normal life is about to end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah's absence from feasts warns that joy is about to be taken away. His withdrawal is a public message, not personal gloom.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says: “Behold, I will cause to cease out of this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.
verses.arminianNotes: "For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says." Arminian readers see the LORD announcing the end of "the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride," a picture of all ordinary joy ceasing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same words appear in Jeremiah 7:34 and 25:10, and are reversed in the promise of 33:11. The book reuses this image, and these notes name the links without merging their settings.

verses.text: It will happen, when you tell this people all these words, and they ask you, ‘Why has the LORD pronounced all this great evil against us?’ or ‘What is our iniquity?’ or ‘What is our sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?’
verses.arminianNotes: "It will happen, when you tell this people all these words." Arminian readers see the people's question, "What is our iniquity?" as revealing how little they recognize their own sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people ask why the LORD has pronounced "all this great evil" against them, as though they were innocent. Their blindness to their sin is itself part of the problem.

verses.text: then you shall tell them, ‘Because your fathers have forsaken me,’ says the LORD, ‘and have walked after other gods, have served them, have worshiped them, have forsaken me, and have not kept my law.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah must answer, "Because your fathers have forsaken me." Arminian readers see the LORD naming the people's history of idolatry and disobedience as the clear cause of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the list: walking after other gods, serving and worshiping them, forsaking the LORD, and not keeping his law. The judgment rests on a long record of covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: You have done evil more than your fathers, for behold, you each walk after the stubbornness of his evil heart, so that you don’t listen to me.
verses.arminianNotes: "You have done evil more than your fathers." Arminian readers see personal responsibility: each walks "after the stubbornness of his evil heart" and refuses to listen. The present generation is not merely suffering for others' sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the stubborn heart lies behind the refusal to listen. The site’s existing box at Genesis 6:5 already treats the shared conviction about the corrupt heart and the fork over inability, and this verse does not open a new one.

verses.text: Therefore I will cast you out of this land into the land that you have not known, neither you nor your fathers. There you will serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.’
verses.arminianNotes: "Therefore I will cast you out of this land." Arminian readers see exile as the consequence of persistent rejection: those who chose other gods will serve them in a foreign land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the bitter justice: "There you will serve other gods day and night." The LORD gives the people over to what they wanted. Both traditions see judgment fitting the sin.
